description: Graph algorithms are used to solve problems represented as networks consisting of nodes (vertices) and connections (edges). These algorithms handle traversals, finding shortest paths, detecting cycles, determining connectivity, and optimizing network costs.
important_details: Graph Representation: Adjacency List (preferred for sparse graphs, O(V+E) space) vs. Adjacency Matrix (preferred for dense graphs, O(V^2) space).
Visited Set: Crucial for preventing infinite loops in graphs with cycles.
Directed vs. Undirected: The direction of edges fundamentally changes how reachability and cycles are calculated.
Weights: Unweighted graphs usually use BFS for shortest paths, while weighted graphs require Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, or Floyd-Warshall.
other_relevant_details: When solving graph problems, first identify if the graph is directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, and cyclic or acyclic. This dictates the choice of algorithm. Many graph problems can also be modeled as 2D grid traversals (e.g., islands, mazes).

variations.description: Breadth-First Search explores the graph level by level, visiting all immediate neighbors before moving deeper. It is the standard algorithm for finding the shortest path in unweighted graphs.
important_details: Data Structure: Uses a Queue (FIFO) to process nodes in the order they are discovered.
Shortest Path: Guarantees the shortest path in terms of the number of edges in unweighted graphs.
Multi-source BFS: Can initialize the queue with multiple starting nodes simultaneously (e.g., Rotten Oranges).
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(V + E). Space Complexity: O(V) for the queue and visited array.

problems.name: As Far From Land as Possible

variations.description: An optimization of BFS for graphs where edge weights are strictly 0 or 1. It uses a Deque instead of a priority queue to achieve O(V+E) shortest path finding.
important_details: Data Structure: Deque (Double-ended queue).
Transition: If edge weight is 0, push to the FRONT of the deque. If weight is 1, push to the BACK.
This maintains the level-order property without the O(log V) overhead of Dijkstra's priority queue.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(V + E). Much faster than Dijkstra for 0/1 weight constraints.

variations.description: Depth-First Search explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. It is highly memory-efficient and used for connectivity, cycle detection, and topological sorting.
important_details: Data Structure: Uses a Stack (LIFO) or recursion (which utilizes the call stack).
Exploration: Dives deep into a path until a dead end is reached, then backtracks.
State Tracking: Often requires tracking 'visited' states. For cycle detection, states are typically 0 (unvisited), 1 (visiting), and 2 (visited).
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(V + E). Space Complexity: O(H) where H is the maximum depth of the recursion tree.

variations.description: Linear ordering of vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge u -> v, vertex u comes before v. Used for dependency resolution.
important_details: Cycle Detection: If a cycle exists, topological sort is impossible.
Kahn's Algorithm (BFS): Computes indegrees. Nodes with 0 indegree are processed first.
DFS Approach: Push nodes to a stack after all their descendants are visited. Pop from stack for the topological order.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(V + E). Space: O(V + E).

variations.description: Maintains a collection of disjoint sets. It provides near O(1) time operations to find the root of an element and union two sets. Used for dynamic connectivity.
important_details: Path Compression: Flattens the tree structure during 'find' operations, ensuring future queries are O(1).
Union by Rank/Size: Attaches the smaller tree to the root of the larger tree, keeping depth logarithmic.
Cycle Detection: If `find(u) == find(v)` before unioning them, adding edge u-v creates a cycle.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(alpha(N)) per operation, where alpha is the Inverse Ackermann function (practically O(1)). Space: O(N).

variations.description: Algorithms for finding the shortest paths between nodes in a weighted graph. Dijkstra handles non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford handles negative weights, and Floyd-Warshall finds all-pairs shortest paths.
important_details: Dijkstra: Uses a Min-Heap. Greedily picks the unvisited node with the smallest distance. Fails on negative edges.
Bellman-Ford: Relaxes all edges V-1 times. Can detect negative cycles. O(V*E).
Floyd-Warshall: DP approach. `dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])`. Great for dense graphs or when querying shortest paths between all pairs. O(V^3).
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: Dijkstra O(E log V), Bellman-Ford O(V*E), Floyd-Warshall O(V^3). Use Floyd-Warshall when graph is small (N <= 100) or transitive closure is needed.

variations.description: Finding a subset of edges in a weighted, undirected graph that connects all vertices together without any cycles and with the minimum possible total edge weight.
important_details: Kruskal's Algorithm: Sorts all edges by weight. Uses Union-Find to add edges if they don't form a cycle. Edge-centric.
Prim's Algorithm: Starts from an arbitrary node. Uses a Min-Heap to greedily add the cheapest edge connecting the current tree to a new vertex. Node-centric.
If the graph is disconnected, an MST cannot be formed (forms a Minimum Spanning Forest).
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity (Prim): O(E log V). Time Complexity (Kruskal): O(E log E).

variations.description: Finding critical edges (Bridges) whose removal disconnects the graph, and critical vertices (Articulation Points) whose removal increases the number of connected components.
important_details: Uses DFS with discovery times (`disc`) and low-link values (`low`).
Bridge condition: During DFS, for edge u-v, if `low[v] > disc[u]`, the edge is a bridge.
Articulation Point condition: For root, if it has >1 child. For non-root u, if `low[v] >= disc[u]`, u is an articulation point.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(V + E). Single pass DFS. Works on directed and undirected graphs but primarily used for undirected.

variations.description: A subgraph where every node is reachable from every other node. Used to compress graphs, detect cycles, or solve 2-SAT problems.
important_details: Kosaraju's Algorithm: 1) DFS on original graph, pushing nodes to a stack by finish time. 2) Reverse the graph. 3) Pop nodes from stack and DFS on reversed graph to find SCCs.
Tarjan's Algorithm: Single DFS using low-link values. A node is an SCC root if `disc[u] == low[u]`.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(V + E). Requires two DFS traversals.

variations.description: Combining binary search with graph traversal. Typically involves binary searching the answer (e.g., max capacity, min effort) and using BFS/DFS to check if the path is feasible under that constraint.
important_details: Monotonicity: If a path exists with max effort X, it also exists for X+1.
Feasibility check: A graph traversal (BFS/DFS) that only uses edges satisfying `edge_weight <= mid`.
Alternative to Dijkstra when you specifically need a min-max or max-min path.

Minimize Max Distance to Gas Station

variations.description: DP or BFS state transitions where the state includes spatial coordinates (x, y) PLUS extra dimensions like remaining steps (k), obstacles eliminated (k), or a bitmask of visited nodes.
important_details: State array: `dp[x][y][k]` or `dp[mask][node]`.
Often combined with BFS (multi-source or stateful BFS).
Bitmask DP is common here where `mask` tracks visited nodes (N <= 15-20).
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity depends on state space. For bitmask it's O(2^N * N^2). For grid + K obstacles, O(M * N * K).
